title: Entry-Level Role Expectations and Professional Behavior

unit.title: Program Orientation, Professionalism, and Healthcare Roles

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe entry-level role expectations for medical office assistants.
- Identify professional behaviors expected in the medical office.
- Recognize the importance of dependability and initiative.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Most medical assistants go to a short training program, like a special school course, to learn the job. It is like taking a class to learn to drive before you get behind the wheel for real.

### Question 2

Medical assistants mostly work in doctors' offices and clinics where people come for check-ups. It is like helping out at the front desk and in the exam rooms of a neighborhood clinic.

### Question 3

Cross-trained means you learn two kinds of jobs at once, like a person who can both cook the food and run the cash register. A medical assistant learns office tasks and hands-on patient tasks.

### Question 4

A medical assistant has a boss with more medical training, like how a student teacher works with a lead teacher watching and guiding them. You follow the doctor's or nurse's instructions.

### Question 5

Administrative duties are the 'paper and phone' jobs, like writing appointments on a calendar. Clinical duties are the 'hands-on with the patient' jobs, like checking a heartbeat.

### Question 6

Clinical duties are the jobs that touch or directly help a patient in the exam room, like getting the room ready and helping the patient get comfortable.

### Question 7

Being detail oriented means paying close attention to the little things, like copying a phone number down correctly. At a doctor's office, a wrong number in a chart could cause real problems.

### Question 8

Interpersonal skills mean being good at talking with and calming people, like being a friendly neighbor who makes someone feel better. Patients at the doctor's office are often nervous, and a kind voice helps.

### Question 9

Most medical assistants work full-time hours, and some work evenings or weekends because clinics can be open when other people are off work.

### Question 10

More medical assistants will be needed in the future because more people need care at doctors' offices and clinics. It is like needing more helpers when a store gets busier.

### Question 11

When you start a new job, someone shows you how that office does things, like learning a new video game's special rules even if you have played games before.

### Question 12

Being dependable means people can trust you to do what you said you would, like a teammate who always shows up for practice. The whole office counts on you to be there.

### Question 13

Being on time means being ready to start when the clock says so, like being in your seat with your pencil ready when class begins.

### Question 14

If you cannot come to work, you tell the person in charge right away, like telling your coach early that you are sick so they can find a substitute player.

### Question 15

Initiative is like seeing the trash is full and taking it out without being asked, but still following the house rules about where the bags go.

### Question 16

Good initiative is raising your hand and asking what to do next, not wandering off or trying a job you have not learned yet.

### Question 17

You should never do a medical job you have not been trained for, even if someone asks. It is like not flying a plane just because a passenger says it is okay.

### Question 18

A friendly 'hello, how can I help you?' with your full attention makes people feel safe, like a store greeter who makes you feel welcome right away.

### Question 19

Dressing professionally means wearing clean clothes that follow the office rules, like wearing the right uniform for your sports team.

### Question 20

At work, your personal phone stays in your pocket, like keeping your toys put away during class so you can pay attention.

### Question 21

A patient's private information is like a secret they trusted you to keep. You should not repeat it, and you should remind others not to either.

### Question 22

When a coach points out a mistake, a good player says thank you and fixes it, because that is how you get better.

### Question 23

If you do not know how to do something, ask someone who does, like raising your hand in class instead of guessing on a test.

### Question 24

If you make a mistake, the honest thing is to tell someone and help fix it, like admitting you dropped the ball in a game instead of pretending it did not happen.

### Question 25

Teamwork is like helping a teammate carry heavy boxes when you see them struggling, doing only the jobs you know how to do safely.

### Question 26

Being an employee is like joining a team where everyone counts on you, instead of doing a project only for your own grade.

### Question 27

Every job has small chores that matter, like putting away equipment after practice. Doing them well shows you are a good teammate.

### Question 28

Learning never stops, like how a video game player learns new levels and updates. Doctors' offices change, so you keep learning new things.

### Question 29

To learn a new skill safely, you watch someone who knows how, then try it with them watching, like learning to bake with an adult nearby.

### Question 30

A performance review is like a report card plus a coach's meeting: it shows what you are doing well and what to work on next.

### Question 31

When you answer the office phone, you say who you are and where the caller reached, like answering 'Hello, this is the Smith house.'

### Question 32

A patient's medical information is private, like a secret you would whisper, not shout across a crowded room.

### Question 33

When you have a problem at work, you tell the right grown-up in charge, like telling your teacher instead of shouting about it to everyone.

### Question 34

A good email has a label that says what it is about, like writing a title on your homework so the teacher knows the topic.

### Question 35

If someone is busy with important work, you wait for a good moment, like waiting for a break in a movie to ask a question.

### Question 36

Work relationships stay at work, like keeping your home address private from customers at a store. Patients should contact the office, not your personal phone.

### Question 37

Reading test results is like reading a tricky map you have not been trained to read. The right move is to let the guide (the doctor) explain it.

### Question 38

Only trained medical professionals give medicine advice, like only a lifeguard tells people how to handle a swimming emergency. You pass the question to the right person.

### Question 39

A rash needs a doctor to figure it out, like a strange noise in a car needs a mechanic. Your job is to write down what the patient says and get the doctor involved.

### Question 40

Giving medicine or a shot is only done when the doctor tells you to, the law allows it, and you have been trained, like only driving the school bus after getting a license.

### Question 41

When the coach gives a clear play, you run that play, and if you do not understand it, you ask before the game starts.

### Question 42

Writing things down correctly and right away is like taking good notes so you do not forget, because the doctor depends on those notes to care for patients.

### Question 43

If someone might be having an emergency, you get help right away, like yelling for a lifeguard when someone is struggling in the water.

### Question 44

Doing a medical task you were never trained for is like driving a fire truck with no license just because the station is busy; it is dangerous and not allowed.

### Question 45

You take the measurement like reading a thermometer, but the doctor decides what the number means, like the coach reading the scoreboard to plan the next play.

### Question 46

The jobs you are allowed to do can be different in different places, like different towns having different rules for what kids may sell at a lemonade stand.

### Question 47

When someone is upset, stay calm and listen, like being the steady friend who does not shout back, and get an adult (a supervisor) if it gets too big.

### Question 48

If you have to say something private, you whisper it or step away so no one else hears, like telling a friend a secret quietly.

### Question 49

If something urgent comes up, you handle it first, like stopping to tell a grown-up about a fire before finishing your chores.

### Question 50

If you did not hear the coach's play, you ask them to say it again instead of guessing and running the wrong way.

### Question 51

A medical assistant is like the helper at the front desk and exam room, while a physician assistant is more like a junior doctor who can treat patients.

### Question 52

Scheduling is like booking a haircut: you need the right person's name, the right stylist, and the right time, or there will be mix-ups.

### Question 53

Working on the computer to keep patient files up to date is an office job, like keeping the class attendance list neat and correct.

### Question 54

A front-office assistant is like the friendly helper at a busy counter who schedules, checks people in, and keeps the paperwork organized.

### Question 55

Filling out insurance forms is paper-and-computer work, like helping fill out a permission slip, not hands-on patient care.

### Question 56

Preparing a patient is like helping someone get comfortable in the dentist's chair; you help and explain, but the dentist decides the treatment.

### Question 57

A lab number is like a code only trained people can read. You pass it to the doctor, who can explain what it really means.

### Question 58

Good body language is like facing someone and looking at them when they talk, which shows you care about what they are saying.

### Question 59

You talk to patients the way you would politely talk to a teacher or neighbor, using kind, clear words.

### Question 60

Personal calls are for break time, like using your phone during recess instead of during class.

### Question 61

If a tool is broken or unsafe, you tell the person in charge, like telling a teacher when the playground equipment is broken.

### Question 62

You are judged on being reliable and doing good work, like being graded on showing up and doing your assignments well.

### Question 63

When many people need help at once, stay calm and help the most urgent first, like a waiter handling several tables politely one step at a time.

### Question 64

You learn a new skill the safe way: someone teaches you, you practice while they watch, and only then do it on your own, like learning to swim with a lifeguard close by.

### Question 65

Even boring jobs matter, like sweeping the floor before a game so no one slips. Doing them well shows you are a good teammate.

### Question 66

The CMAA is like a badge for being great at the office side of the job: scheduling, records, and helping patients at the desk.

### Question 67

The notes you write are like the clues a detective (the doctor) uses to solve a case; if the clues are wrong, the answer may be wrong too.

### Question 68

Collecting a sample is done the careful, clean way the office teaches, like following a recipe exactly so the food turns out right and no one gets sick.

### Question 69

Private talks happen in private places, like having a secret conversation in a quiet corner instead of the middle of the playground.

### Question 70

Initiative is like cleaning up your area without being told, but still asking the teacher before doing something big like rearranging the whole room.

### Question 71

At work you need sturdy, closed shoes, like wearing sneakers for gym class instead of flip-flops, so you do not get hurt.

### Question 72

Following through is doing what you said you would, like actually returning the book you promised to lend a friend.

### Question 73

If someone says you were unkind, you listen and think about how to do better, like a player listening when a coach says their passes were sloppy.

### Question 74

Sharing a patient's private information outside work is like telling someone's secret to the whole neighborhood; it is a big no-no.

### Question 75

If you are not sure about a cleaning or safety rule, you stop and ask, like checking the rulebook before handling something dangerous.
